prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I have moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and I want to be clear that the reason is the argument and not the five-to-one count. B019 remains the strongest case on the list: the chain from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through the identity and actions of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to drugs with confirmed glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit, is mature and stable, and no member argues for delay. What persuaded me is that the prize is for a discovery, and the three contributions I can most cleanly separate are Holst's human physiology, Drucker's work on proglucagon-derived peptides and their receptor biology, and the identification of the biologically active form of the hormone. Knudsen's acylation and albumin-binding step is real and decisive for the drugs that exist, but it is optimisation of a principle that was already defined, and the therapeutic step has no target without the active peptide. I can carry that in the citation by saying that the discoveries made the therapies possible, which respects the translational outcome without placing a drug-development name inside the three slots.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point, and my change does not remove it. Habener is outside the credited list and plausibly has a claim to the early peptide history, so any trio looks incomplete to someone. Mojsov's priority is contested, and I still cannot adjudicate it from this record. My concern is that a contested priority is treated by others as a reason for diligence and by me earlier as a reason for caution, and the committee should settle that openly before the vote and not carry it as an unexamined assumption. Leaving out Knudsen also means that the prize does not name the person whose analogues became liraglutide and semaglutide, and a reader could say we cited physiology while the patients received engineering. A second concern is that a physiology-only trio could look to some like a prize that shies away from the drug. I accept both costs as smaller than the cost of blurring discovery and development inside one part, and I would not favour a second part at the price of splitting the GLP-1 names.

responses.point: Thomas argues that replacing Mojsov with Knudsen changes what the prize is for, from the discovery of the active hormone and its physiology to the engineering of the pharmaceutical, that a disputed priority calls for diligence and not omission, and that he would support Knudsen if diligence on Mojsov proved unfavourable.
responses.response: I accept this argument and it is the main reason I have moved. If the prize is for the discovery, then identification of the active form is the step on which both the physiology and the pharmacology depend, and Knudsen's step has no target without it. I agree that a contested priority is a reason to read the primary record carefully and not a reason to omit. I keep your condition as my own: if the committee's diligence on Mojsov relative to Habener came back clearly unfavourable, I would reopen the third name, and at that point I would prefer to consider Knudsen over an arbitrary substitution. Absent that finding, I now stand with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov.

responses.point: Abdel says the prize is for a discovery, that dropping Mojsov removes the contributor who ties the peptide's identity to its biological activity, and that if the committee wants translational credit the principled route is to ask whether a second part is warranted, not to swap names inside one part.
responses.response: The distinction you draw between swapping a name inside one part and creating a second part is the one I had not made cleanly in round 1, and it is right. Using the third slot to carry the drug step was an indirect way of answering a question that should be argued openly. I have now answered it: I do not think a second part for the drug step is warranted, because the three-person limit applies to the union and a second part would force a split of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov that I cannot defend on the merits. So the translational outcome goes into the citation language and not into the credited names. I also continue to share your view that optogenetics is a poor candidate this year on attribution grounds, though for me that is a reservation about crediting six names and not about its importance.

responses.point: Per, as chair, frames the citation around physiology and the active peptide, says that analogue design is optimisation within a company programme, and that if the committee wants to credit the drugs it should argue that explicitly and not reach it indirectly through the choice of names.
responses.response: I now agree with the second half of your point most strongly. I argued for crediting the drugs indirectly through Knudsen, and I should have argued it directly. Having thought about it, I am willing to argue it directly and I come out against it for this year: the citation can say that the discoveries made incretin-based therapies possible, and that is as far as I would go. I still do not fully accept the label 'optimisation' as dismissive, because durable half-life was not routine, but where the work was done is not the issue; the issue is that the prize should name the people who established what the hormone is and what it does. On your question about whether the lack of primary-record verification justifies deferral, I would say no: a documented caveat on Habener and on Mojsov's priority is sufficient, since none of us argues that the physiology or the maturity is in doubt.

responses.point: Rickard ranks B028 as his fallback and the best second part if a two-part prize is wanted, but does not think a two-part prize is needed when B019 alone is so strong, and notes that a citation centred on the drug class would enlarge the Mojsov and Habener question.
responses.response: I agree that B019 alone is sufficient, and that a second part is not needed. My own reason is about the three-person limit: B028 with Walter and Mori is the cleanest attribution on the list, but adding it would require dropping one of the GLP-1 names, and I do not see which one could be dropped without damaging the chain. I also agree with your point that a drug-centred citation would make the Mojsov and Habener problem larger, since the priority question would then bear on the central claim and not only on the third name. That is a further reason for the physiology-and-active-form wording. B028 stays as my first fallback if the committee decides that the GLP-1 attribution cannot be settled, because there the credit is easier to defend.

responses.point: Marie says the discovery to be recognised is the physiology (what the hormone is, where it comes from, what it does), that Knudsen's work builds on that and competes for slots with those who established the biology, and that she would revisit if the committee saw the prize as chiefly about the therapy.
responses.response: I agree with your framing and have changed my position accordingly. I would add one qualification to your counterpoint that the discovery would not have changed medicine without durable analogues: that is true, but it is a statement about impact and not about who made the discovery, and the prize is for discovery. I do not consider the prize chiefly about the therapy, so your condition for revisiting is not met for me. On your fallback of B014 or B032 if GLP-1 is judged unresolvable, I would take B014 ahead of B032, with June and Sadelain only, because I am less persuaded that anti-TNF therapy is a discovery of equal standing.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide, relative to Habener, can be established well enough from the record to support naming her; I cannot verify it and have not changed that view, only the weight I put on it.
Whether the committee will accept a citation that mentions the therapies without crediting the drug-development step, or whether it would read as under-crediting the therapeutic achievement.
Whether Habener's omission from the credited list should be handled by a documented caveat alone, as I now think, or by a change of configuration.
If B019 were set aside, whether June and Sadelain alone, with Eshhar's earlier chimeric receptor concept uncredited, is a defensible B014 or whether B028 is the better fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from my profile, and no member has disclosed one that requires recusal. For the record, my documented connections are co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and about eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg (the count has not been audited), neither of which involves a shortlisted candidate. I have not inferred any tie from shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation or from field overlap. My disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
